extracted.intended_audience: novelists, painters, and writers seeking historically accurate/realistic depictions of peasants and social types
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for depicting peasant characters, speech, customs, and social behaviour with historical truth and social realism; includes methods of research and cautions against common writerly mistakes. Useful for fiction writers and visual artists aiming for authentic historical/ethnographic portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek real peasant models for medieval authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: A painter who wants to draw mediæval characters with historic truth must seek his models among the peasantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting historical or mediæval types, use living peasant physiognomies and customs as models rather than contemporary cultured types; the reviewer notes that medieval sculptures represent the same regional 'type' now found among peasants. Anti-pattern: inventing anachronistic or urbanized features for medieval rural characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent peasants as less individualized, more typal
rubrics_metrics.description: The race had not attained to a high degree of individualization in features and expression; the cultured man acts more as an individual, the peasant more as one of a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization should reflect stronger communal uniformity in manner, dress, and thought among peasants; avoid over-personalizing them with the same nuanced interiority given to cultivated characters. Example: old German painters gave heads greater uniformity for this reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve provincial speech and dialectal particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: In the cultivated world each individual has his style of speaking and writing. But among the peasantry it is the race, the district, the province, that has its style—namely, its dialect, its phraseology, its proverbs, and its songs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render peasant dialogue using local dialect features, proverbs, and communal phraseology rather than idiosyncratic individual registers. Use region-specific sayings and songs to indicate group identity. Anti-pattern: giving every peasant a distinct polished individual manner of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical-lingual survivals (names, calendar-terms) accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiarity of the peasant’s language consists chiefly in his retention of historical peculiarities... He prefers any proper name that may be given to a day in the calendar, rather than the abstract date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include local naming practices, archaic baptismal names, and calendar-based names when relevant; these details can locate characters topographically and historically. Example: continuity of certain proper names can be used as a regional identifier. Anti-pattern: erasing such survivals in favour of modern conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not transfer urban/cultured emotional life to peasants
rubrics_metrics.description: The German novelists... transfer their own feelings to ploughmen and woodcutters, and give them both joys and sorrows of which they know nothing. With him general custom holds the place of individual feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing the refined sentimental responses, romantic inner lives, or psychological subtleties typical of urban characters to peasants. Show that custom and communal norms often trump individualized emotion. Example: peasant family obligations are pragmatic, not tender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show conservatism rooted in practical costs and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The unwillingness of the peasant to adopt innovations has a not unreasonable foundation in the fact that for him experiments are practical, not theoretical, and must be made with expense of money instead of brains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying peasant resistance to change, explain it through concrete economic/practical constraints and risk, not mere backwardness. Example: reluctance to adopt braces vs. tight leather belts; anti-pattern: treating conservatism as irrational obstinacy without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict traditional customs even when inconvenient
rubrics_metrics.description: The peasant’s adherence to the traditional has much greater inconvenience than that entailed by a paucity of proper names... wearing seven petticoats to field-labour because it is traditionally correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use persistent, sometimes inconvenient customs (clothing, food habits, household rituals) to show historical continuity and cultural meaning. Such details reveal attachment to ancestry. Anti-pattern: removing such quirks for 'practical' realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray local feuds and nicknaming as historically rooted social practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Between many villages an historical feud, once perhaps the occasion of much bloodshed, is still kept up under the milder form of an occasional round of cudgelling and the launching of traditional nicknames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include inherited rivalries, nicknames, and ritualized violence as communal institutions whose original causes may be forgotten. These provide texture and plausible social dynamics. Anti-pattern: treating them as episodic eccentricities with no social logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show legal vanity and litigation as part of peasant honor and custom
rubrics_metrics.description: The farmer’s lawsuit is his point of honor... The litigious peasant piques himself... on his knowledge of the law, and this vanity is the chief impulse to many a lawsuit. Custom with him holds the place of sentiment, of theory, and in many cases of affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing scenes of peasant litigation or legal disputes, frame them as expressions of honor, pride in custom, and local knowledge, not mere money-seeking. Consider pacing (peasants avoid law in summer) as part of realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict political action as local, practical, and non-theoretical
rubrics_metrics.description: The peasant... has always plenty of grievances in his pocket, but he does not generalize those grievances... their petitions contain no 'universal rights of man,' but simply their own particular affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray peasant political engagement as driven by immediate local interests (toll-houses, taxes, forest rights) and tangible benefits, not abstract ideology. Example: during revolutions peasants act for concrete gains (wood, land), often misunderstanding wider aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show naïveté in revolutionary ideas as historically framed expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The peasant contemplated 'partition' by the light of an historical reminiscence... He understood by 'partition' that the State lands... would be divided among the communes... That he should give up a single clod of his own had never entered the mind of the peasant communist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting peasants attracted to radical schemes, emphasize historical frames of reference and concrete expectations rather than doctrinal comprehension. Use misinterpretation of slogans for narrative irony or conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow social change to be gradual and historically embedded
rubrics_metrics.description: What has grown up historically can only die out historically, by the gradual operation of necessary laws... The external conditions which society has inherited from the past are but the manifestation of inherited internal conditions in the human beings who compose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative arcs of social development should respect slow, organic change: characters and institutions evolve in tandem. Avoid sudden, theory-driven transformations that ignore historical roots. Method: show small continuities and gradual shifts rather than abrupt wholesale reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the life-affirming qualities of historical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Your language may be a perfect medium of expression to science, but will never express life... With the anomalies and inconveniences of historical language you will have parted with its music and its passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-simplify or 'rationalize' historical or regional language for clarity's sake at the cost of expressive power. Retain idiom, archaisms, and subtle associations to convey imagination, humor, and character. Anti-pattern: inventing a sterilized, utilitarian tongue that communicates only propositional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inductive field observation as a research method
rubrics_metrics.description: He began his wanderings over the hills and plains of Germany for the sake of obtaining, in immediate intercourse with the people, that completion of his historical, political, and economical studies which he was unable to find in books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers aiming for realistic social portraits should conduct firsthand observation and prolonged contact with communities (walking, talking, living among them) rather than relying exclusively on secondary sources. This produces nuanced, grounded detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid universalizing social theories across distinct societies
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal social policy has no validity except on paper... The conditions of German society are altogether different from those of French, of English, or of Italian society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social fiction or social-critique writing, resist transplanting one nation's social model wholesale onto another; attend to national, regional, and historical specificities. Anti-pattern: applying a single social theory or typology to heterogeneous settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray peasant family life as pragmatic and duty-bound rather than sentimental
rubrics_metrics.description: The peasant never questions the obligation of family ties—he questions no custom—but tender affection, as it exists among the refined part of mankind, is almost as foreign to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict marriage, filial obligations, and eldercare in peasant societies as practical arrangements and social duties, often lacking the romanticized tenderness common in refined-class fiction. Use folk proverbs and moral tales (e.g., ungrateful children) to illustrate communal moral lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bodily, habitual traits to indicate historical character
rubrics_metrics.description: Some years ago a peasant youth... having never in his life slept in a bed, when he had got into one for the first time began to cry like a child... The genuine peasant is never ashamed of his rank and calling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include embodied habits—sleeping practices, clothing, food preferences, physical robustness or stoicism—to ground characters historically and socially. Such traits can explain reactions (homesickness, inability to adapt) and social attitudes (pride in rank).
